catalog_quote: [Rice 1983, pp. 17-18; the page's stress underlines are listed under Secondary stress] The stress system of Fort Nelson Slave is basically one of alternating stress. Stressed vowels are underlined. (3) nímáli 'tent' dɛchį tah gotth'įlɛ 'clearing in trees' gotthįlɛ 'clearing' In two syllable words, both bear stress. (4) dɛchį 'stick' tlįcho 'horse' Possessive prefixes are ignored with respect to stress placement for most speakers. (5) sįní 'my face' sɛdɛchinɛ̨ 'my stick' chi chudhɛ̨ 'duck down' Suffixes often do not receive stress when phrase final. (6) chi chudhɛ̨ 'duck down' kǫ túɛ̨ 'alcohol' mɛhchinɛ̨ 'toboggan' When non-phrase final, the suffix is stressed. (7) chi chudhɛ̨ łǫ 'lots of duck down' mɛhchinɛ̨ dhɛh 'sleigh wrapper' kǫtúɛ̨ ts'ɛhtsini 'brew' [Rice 2010, pp. 171-172] In Slave, too, the stem plays an important role in determining accent placement. In the South Slavey dialect, quantity distinctions have generally been neutralized, and accent is on the stem vowel. ... (23) South Slavey (dialect of Slave; data from Rice 1989 unless otherwise indicated) ... The stem vowel is stressed, whether a suffix is present or not (23b, d, e), and whether that suffix ends in a consonant (23e) or a vowel (23b, d). In the Hare dialect of Slave the position of accent differs in nouns and verbs. Nouns are accented on the stem (24a), as in South Slavey; verbs have prestem accent, as in (24b)
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had
sweep_summary: South Slavey is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Rice 1987 'Metrical structure in a tone language: the foot in Slave (Athapaskan)', resolves to CLS 23 vol. 2 pp. 239-252 (citation confirmed from four bibliographies) and to ANLA typescript CA976Rc1987 (ca. 27 pp., languages 'Comparative Athabaskan, Hare, Slave', no file); Glottolog's ANLA URL is dead, and no open copy exists (HathiTrust, archive.org, Crossref, Google Books no-preview) — only its first sentence was readable, and the foot argument is probably Hare-based, so relevance to South Slavey stress is unclear (priority medium). The best first-hand statement found is Rice 2010 (Survey of Word Accentual Patterns, pp. 171-172), assembled from Google Books snippets: 'In the South Slavey dialect, quantity distinctions have generally been neutralized, and accent is on the stem vowel.. The stem vowel is stressed, whether a suffix is present or not', citing Rice 1989 as data source and contrasting Hare. Rice 1989 A Grammar of Slave p. 46 (snippets copied from the slav1253 folder) says stress is not distinctive in Slave and gives the pre-stem/stem rule for Hare only. A South Slavey record would be 'morphological, stem-vowel stress (non-distinctive, intensity-cued)', consistent with the reclassify already recommended for the sister Slave record slav1253. Everything downloaded is under with. for the session was exhausted

In the South Slavey dialect, quantity distinctions have generally been neutralized, and accent is on the stem vowel. The stem vowel is underlined; an acute accent marks high tone, and the hyphen indicates a stem boundary. (23) South Slavey (dialect of Slave; data from Rice 1989 unless otherwise indicated) a. ch-'ke 'boy' b. 'lu-e 'fish' c. ne-'do 'you sg. drink' d. de-'tsil-e ... new_statements.rule_in_words: South Slavey word accent (stress) is morphologically fixed: it falls on the stem (root) vowel of nouns and verbs alike, regardless of whether a suffix follows; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed. Rice 2018 (p. 232, snippet) restates this as prominence on the first syllable of the root, with no weight sensitivity because historical vowel-length contrasts have been neutralized. The reference grammar (Rice 1989:46) adds that stress is not distinctive in Slave and that a prefix vowel bearing a floating plus lexical high tone gets extra intensity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in Rice 2010. Rice 1983 (Fort Nelson Slave report, pp. 17-18, full scan held by the project) describes 'alternating stress' from the stem-initial syllable rightward (both syllables of disyllabic words stressed, possessive prefixes skipped, suffix stressed only when non-phrase-final); Rice 2018 table p. 250 codes Slavey as 'syllabic trochee' on the root.
new_statements.exceptions: Hare (North Slavey) verbs have prestem accent instead (Rice 2010:172; Rice 1989:46; Hargus & Rice 2005:35). Rice 1989:46: stress is not a distinctive feature in Slave; a prefix vowel with lexical high tone that also receives a shifted high tone 'has extra stress, or is more intense'; in Fort Nelson Slave possessive prefixes are ignored 'for most speakers' and suffixes are unstressed phrase-finally (Rice 1983:17-18).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stems with prefixes and suffixes; nouns and verbs); Rice 1983 additionally notes phrase-position effects on suffix stress. Rice is the field linguist for all Slave dialects and the 2010 chapter uses her own grammar data (Rice 1989), so the statement is first-hand although it appears in a typological survey chapter. Text recovered from overlapping Google Books snippet windows saved to disk, not from a page scan; the two deciding sentences are complete in the windows.
new_statements.identity_note: Rice 2010's 'South Slavey (dialect of Slave)' is the NWT Slavey of Fort Simpson/Dehcho, i.e. sout2959; her grammar (Rice 1989) and the 1993 sketch cover the whole Slave dialect complex (South Slavey, Bearlake, Hare, Mountain; our check's family-level directory is slav1253, and Hare/Bearlake/Mountain = North Slavey nort2942). The full-scan first-hand stress description held by the project (Rice 1983, Part 4) is for Fort Nelson Slave, the British Columbia dialect of South Slavey (Fort Nelson, Kahntah, Fontas), which Rice says differs from NWT Slavey in several features; the StressTyp2 'Slave' entry and Gordon 2016 report the Hare (North Slavey) verb pattern as if it were general Slave.

new_statements.reading: South Slavey word stress/accent is morphologically fixed on the stem vowel: the (typically final or near-final) stem syllable is stressed whether or not a suffix follows, and syllable weight plays no role because quantity contrasts have been neutralised. Written by Keren Rice, the primary describer of Slave, citing her own 1989 grammar as the data source; reachable only as overlapping Google Books snippets (pp. 171-172), so the full example set (23a-e) should be read from the chapter itself. Rice 1989 p. 46 adds that stress is not distinctive in Slave and that intensity is its main correlate, and describes a different pre-stem-verb / stem-noun pattern for the Hare dialect (North Slavey), which Rice 2010 also contrasts with South Slavey.

Amsterdam/Philadelphia: John Benjamins. DOI 10.1075/cilt.269.07kra (with editors' 'Preface to Michael Krauss' article', pp. 47-49, and Krauss's own preface, pp. 51-53).
tone_statements.quote: [p. 11] The basic C-H pattern with high tone from constriction or glottalization, and low tone in its absence, has been called “high-marked” by Leer [...] The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Hare-Bearlake-Mountain, and also Chilcotin. [p. 58] Hare, Mountain, Bearlake and Slave, closely related and largely mutually intelligible, all show very regular development of high-marked tone. In Hare the stem-tone assimilates to that of the suffix, but in Bearlake and Slavey there is no such assimilation, except apparently in the case of “younger brother”. Also in both Bearlake and Slavey “egg” shows irregular low stem-tone
tone_statements.summary: Two-tone (H vs L) high-marked Athabaskan system: high tone reflects Proto-Athabaskan vowel constriction (glottalization), low tone its absence; regular reflexes in Slavey nouns, no Hare-type stem-to-suffix tone assimilation.

sources.quote: Stress is not a distinctive feature [in] Slave. In the Hare dialect, there are stress-like properties which are predictable. What might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun. A stressed vowel is generally acoustically more intense than an unstressed vowel, and intensity is in fact the primary phonetic correlate of stress. See chapter 8. In prefixes in all dialects, a high tone may fall on a vowel with lexical high tone. That vowel then has extra stress, or is more intense.

sources.note: Grammar Part One, Vowels: every vowel bears high or low tone, high marked with acute; VV sequences H+L give a falling and L+H a rising contour. Later sections (pp. 31-32, 'Verb stems') state that imperfective and perfective stems can differ in tone, that the nasal perfective suffix correlates with low tone on the stem vowel ('the suffixed perfective stem always has low tone'), and describe high tone spreading/raising on prefixes before conjugation markers in the paradigm chapters (grammatical tone).

tone.quote: [p. 11] The basic C-H pattern with high tone from constriction or glottalization, and low tone in its absence, has been called “high-marked” by Leer [...] The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Hare-Bearlake-Mountain, and also Chilcotin. [p. 58] Hare, Mountain, Bearlake and Slave, closely related and largely mutually intelligible, all show very regular development of high-marked tone. In Hare the stem-tone assimilates to that of the suffix, but in Bearlake and Slavey there is no such assimilation, except apparently in the case of “younger brother”. Also in both Bearlake and Slavey “egg” shows irregular low stem-tone
tone.summary: Two-tone (H vs L) high-marked Athabaskan system: high tone reflects Proto-Athabaskan vowel constriction (glottalization), low tone its absence; regular reflexes in Slavey nouns, no Hare-type stem-to-suffix tone assimilation.
tone.says: Comparative account of Athabaskan tonogenesis from ca. 110 noun etyma. Slave/Slavey is placed in the acute 'high-marked' area (PA constricted/glottalized full vowels > high tone, non-constricted > low), together with Chipewyan, Beaver, Kaska, N. Tutchone and Hare-Bearlake-Mountain (p. 11); Hare-Mountain-Bearlake-Slave 'all show very regular development of high-marked tone'; unlike Hare, Slavey (and Bearlake) show no assimilation of stem tone to the suffix tone except apparently in 'younger brot…
